div.p: To dedicate treatises on horsemanship, or hunting, or fishing, or farming to men who long to be engaged in such pursuits is, I think, fitting; but a study of the art of generalship, Quintus Veranius, belongs to the Romans, and most of all to those Romans who have been allotted the rank of the senatorial aristocracy and who, by the wisdom of Augustus Caesar, are adorned with consular and praetorian authority, both because of an education in which they have no small experience, and because of the dignity of their ancestors.

I say, then, that we should choose the general not by judging by birth, as we choose priests, nor by wealth, as we choose the masters of the gymnasium, but as a man self-controlled, temperate, vigilant, frugal, hardened to labour, intelligent, free from the love of money, neither young nor old, the father of children if it so happen, capable of speaking, and of good repute.
Let the good general, then, be envied if he is also nobly born and rich, but let not the poor man with virtue be rejected, even if he is not of brilliant stock.

Let him choose either counsellors who will share with him in all deliberation and take part in his judgement, men who attend him for this very purpose, or let him summon the most honoured of the officers themselves and take counsel with them; for whatever a man has thought out alone, as his own, he does not securely make his own.

I say that the beginnings of war should above all be undertaken prudently, and that one should make it plain to all that he goes to war with justice on his side; for then the gods too become favourable allies to the soldiers, and men oppose the dangers more readily.
Let the general lead out his forces purified, by whatever purifications the sacred laws or the seers prescribe, expelling every public defilement and every private pollution that cleaves to each man.
Chapter 6

Let him lead the whole army in formation, even if he is not yet about to engage, but is crossing by a long road and accomplishing a march of many days, both in friendly and in hostile territory: through the friendly, that the troops may be accustomed to keep their ranks and to hold together their own companies and to follow their leaders; through the hostile, against the sudden ambushes that occur, lest at a critical moment, thrown into confusion and running about, and rushing one against another, they accomplish nothing, being caught off guard, and suffer many grievous things, but rather may be at once well disposed for marching and ready for battle, having the watchword and keeping one another in sight in their ranks.

Whenever he is about to make his passage through narrows, or to lead his army through mountainous and difficult country, it is necessary, by sending forward some part of the force, to seize beforehand both the passes and the entrances of the defiles, lest the enemy forestall him and, occupying the heights, prevent the army from making its way through.

When encamping in the enemy's country, let him throw round a palisade and a ditch, even if he intends to set up his camp for but a day; for such a camp is free from regret and safe against the sudden and unexpected assaults. Let him post sentries, even if he believes the enemy far off, as though they were near.

It is useful too, and a means of safety to an army, not to remain in the same camp, unless it be wintering and the camp has, because of the season, become as it were a city with its tents; for the discharges of the body's necessities, taking place in the same spots, send up corrupted vapours and alter even the quality of the surrounding air.

Therefore it is the part of a good general to provide useful things at the time when the necessities of pitched battle are not pressing, and to impose even useless tasks for the sake of bodily exercise. For armies, even if exceedingly worn out, find rest enough in the trial that is not through real dangers leading to the actual contest. Let him exercise them in some such ways as follow.
Since often, when men sacrifice, the victims are favourable as for a battle, yet through that battle sometimes foreshow the whole destruction of armies, I think it most necessary to speak about this.

When encamped opposite the enemy's palisade, let him not neglect the timely taking of the morning meal; for if he considers that it lies with himself to draw up the army for battle when he wishes, and whenever he pleases, let him order his forces to take their meal; but if he happens to have come into such necessity—through the nature of the ground, or weakness of the palisade, or some other causes—that it is left to the enemy to lead out their forces whenever they choose and to impose upon him the necessity of taking up arms and drawing up in opposition, let him not hesitate to give the signal for the morning meal even at dawn, lest the enemy forestall him and lay upon him, fasting, the necessity of fighting.

When some despondency and fear falls upon armies—whether because a reinforcement has come to the enemy, or because they have gained some advantage—then above all let the general appear to the soldiers cheerful and glad and undismayed.

Just as encouragement of an army has at the right time done good, so too fear has been of service. For when a camp grows slack and disobedient to its leaders, one should hint at the danger from the enemy, making most fearsome their lying in wait; for thus he will make the men not cowardly, but safe; for in despondency one must take courage, and in slackness one must fear; for the one makes cowards brave, the other makes the bold forethoughtful.

The order of war is not one, but many and various—according to the kinds of arms, and the troops, and the places, and the opponents, the differences of which the general will know on the very occasions; but those things which are not least suited to many formations, apart from those that must be conceived on the occasions themselves, these I shall run through as in summary.
Chapter 16

The general will array his cavalry not so much as he wishes as he is compelled; for he will set his own against the enemy's cavalry. Let him station them, for the most part, in pitched battles upon the wing, that, attacking both in front and from the flank, and using greater room—beyond which no others are stationed—they may be able to make full use of the cavalry's skill.
Chapter 17

The light-armed—javelin-men and archers and slingers—let him station first, before the phalanx; for if they are behind, they will do more harm to their own men than to the enemy, and if they are in the midst, they will have their own skill rendered ineffectual, being able neither to retire step by step, because of the upraising of the javelins, nor to cast on the run, since others are in front and at their feet; nor again can the slingers complete the whirl of the sling all around, since friendly hoplites stand at their side and strike against the swing; and the archers, advancing before the others, shoot their missiles into the very bodies and at their mark, but when behind the companies or in their very midst, they shoot upward, so that the missile has force for the upward flight, but again, even if it falls upon the enemy's heads, it is spent and does not much harm the foe.
Chapter 18

If it should happen that the battle takes place in ground having some parts low and some hilly, then above all let him station the light-armed in the rough places; and indeed, even if he himself has occupied the level ground while certain parts of the enemy's phalanx hold the rising ground, let him lead the light-armed up against these; for they more easily withdraw to the rough ground after casting, and most easily run back up the slopes, if they happen to be nimble.
Chapter 19

Let there be intervals along the ranks, that, when they have emptied their missiles while the enemy still advance, before the phalanxes come to close quarters, the light-armed, wheeling about, may pass in good order through the middle of the phalanx and be carried back without confusion to the rear; for it is not safe for them to circle round the whole army and bend about by the wing—for perhaps the enemy will forestall them in the meantime by closing with them and catching them in the middle—nor to force a way through the close-packed ranks, falling upon the arms and producing confusion among the formations as one man jostles against another.

If he himself be in want of the support of light-armed, while the enemy have the advantage in this, let the front-rank men march in close order with shields the height of a man, so as to cover their whole bodies with their length, while those behind these and behind them, down to the last, raise their shields over their heads and hold them so until they come within range of the missiles; for thus, roofed over, so to speak, they will suffer no harm from the marksmen.

Wishing to guard against encirclements, let him neither so extend his force in length as to make the phalanx wholly weak and shallow—for it quickly comes about that the enemy break through it and make a passage, and no longer work by the wing with their encirclements, but, having burst through the middle, get to the rear of their opponents; let him not only guard against suffering this, but also seek to do it, if he perceives the enemy's phalanx weak and thin—nor let him so contract his line at the rear, drawing it into great depth, that the enemy may most easily outflank it and take it within their wings.

Let him have somewhere also picked soldiers stationed apart from the phalanx, as reserves of the battle, for the hard-pressed parts of the force, that he may bring up help ready to hand; and otherwise too fresh men coming up have done no small service against those already wearied; for they have both recovered those of their friends who were already worn out and have set upon the enemy when these were spent, while they themselves were fresh.

And at some time, riding along, let him shout to his friends—if he happen to be on the right wing—"Men, those on the left are conquering the right wing of the enemy"; and if he be on the left, let him say that the friendly right wing is conquering, whether this be in truth happening or not; for indeed it is necessary to speak the falsehood where "a great strife has arisen." So again, when the enemy's commander is far off, either on the other wing or holding the centre of the phalanx, let him shout, "The enemy's general is dead," or "the king," or whoever it may be.

It is the part of a prudent general also to station brothers beside brothers, friends beside friends, lovers beside their beloved; for when what is in danger nearby is dearer, of necessity the one who loves fights more readily for his neighbour; and indeed a man, ashamed not to repay the kindness he has received, is ashamed to leave behind his benefactor and be the first himself to begin a flight.
Chapter 25

Let him give every order and watchword and countersign through the officers; for to proclaim it, going round, to all is the mark of a private man and an utterly inexperienced one, and time is wasted in the proclaiming, and there is confusion as all at once question one another; then one has added something more than the general said, and another has taken away from what was said, through ignorance.

Let the countersign not be spoken by voice, but be given by the body—by a nod of the hand, or a clashing of arms, or an inclining of the spear, or a sweep of the sword—that, when at some time confusion arises, they may trust not only the spoken watchword (for this the enemy too can often catch by overhearing) but also the countersign.

Let him order both retreats and pursuits to be made in formation, that, on the one hand, being less liable to error, they may suffer less harm, not falling man by man, scattered in their flights, into the enemy's hands, and, on the other, succeeding more, they may do more harm, appearing in stronger array against the fleeing in ranks and companies, and besides be safer; for often the enemy, seeing them advance in disorder, have come to their senses again and, recovering their order by a turn-about, have made the pursuit run the other way. And in general let him say to them that nothing is better than to remain in formation, nor anything more perilous than to break it.
Chapter 28

Let it be a care to the general to draw up the army brilliant in its arms; and this care is easy, by bidding the men sharpen their swords and burnish their helmets and breastplates; for the advancing companies appear more terrible by the flashing of their arms, and the many terrors that fall through the eyes upon the soul throw the enemy into confusion.
Chapter 29
Let him lead the army on also with a war-cry, and sometimes even at a run; for both the sight and the shout and the clash of arms unhinge the minds of the opponents.

Then, having reckoned which troops he must set against which, and in what manner—like a good physician who, having first discerned the body's sickness, brings against it the remedies—let him draw up his force as may seem best to be advantageous to him; for generals are often compelled to order and array their own armies with reference both to the arms of their opponents and to their nations and to their characters.
Chapter 31

If the enemy be superior in cavalry, let him, if possible, choose rough and narrow ground, beside mountains, which is least suited to horsemen, or let him avoid battle as much as he can, until he finds suitable places fitting to his own affairs.

As for those generals who either pull down their own fortifications, or cross rivers, or put cliffs and chasms behind their own men, that, remaining, they may conquer, or, should they wish to flee, may perish—these I can neither altogether praise nor blame; for everything done at hazard is rather of daring than of judgement, and has had more share in fortune than in calculation.

Let the general himself fight more with forethought than with daring, or even altogether refrain from coming to hand-to-hand combat with the enemy; for even if he should bring into the struggles unsurpassed courage, he can do an army no such service by fighting as he can do it harm by dying; for a general's judgement is stronger than his bodily strength; for by bodily courage even a common soldier can do some great deed, but by forethought of judgement no one but a general can devise something better.

Having recalled the army from the battle, let him first render to the gods sacrifices and processions, such as it is possible to offer at the moment, promising to render the customary thank-offerings after the complete victory of the war; then let him honour those who proved the best in the dangers with gifts and honours, such as custom allows, and punish those shown to be base.
Plundering is not to be permitted at every battle, nor always of everything, but of some things, of others not; and of captive persons least of all—these the general should sell.

Let him take thought for the burial of the dead, making no excuse of time or season or place or fear, whether he happen to be victorious or defeated; for piety toward the departed is holy, and the proof of it to the living is also necessary.
Having made a truce, let him neither attack nor be himself off his guard; but let him keep his quiet toward the enemy as in peace, and his safety against suffering as in war.

Let him deal kindly and honestly with the cities that come over, if any are the first to entrust themselves; for thus he would win over the rest as well. For the hope of obtaining the same treatment, alluring the many, draws them on to put themselves willingly into his hands.

For assaults and the nocturnal seizures of cities through treachery, one must not be inexperienced in the movement of the fixed stars across the heavens by night, since often he will find his attempts ineffectual.

A siege demands the courage of the soldiers, the inventiveness of generalship, and the preparation of engines; yet let it be safe and no less unforeseen by the besieged than theirs is by him; for what is plotted against, whenever it knows what evil it is meeting,

They would least venture this if the besieging general posted companies at the gates and the small sally-ports to ward off the sudden sallies of the enemy, since otherwise they might often attack those outside unnoticed.

For fear is a lying prophet, and will think that the things it dreads are also coming to pass; and everything by night, even if it be small, is more fearsome to the besieged; for no one says what he sees, because of the darkness, but everyone what he hears; and when one or two enemies somewhere appear on the wall, supposing that the whole army has already mounted the walls, they have turned and fled, leaving the battlements and gates deserted.

I have dedicated this treatise to them first not as men inexperienced in generalship, but emboldened most of all by this consideration: that an ignorant mind fails to recognize even what another man does well, whereas knowledge bears witness in favour of what is rightly done.
Self-controlled, that he may not, drawn aside by natural pleasures, abandon his care for matters of the greatest moment.

Once chosen, let the general be honest, affable, ready, unflustered, neither so lenient as to be despised nor so terrible as to be hated, that he may neither relax the army by indulgences nor estrange it by terrors.
For a judgement that is unaided and left to itself peers anxiously about its own discovery, whereas one confirmed by the testimony of those near at hand is made trustworthy as being free from danger.

For knowing that they are not the aggressors but the defenders, with souls conscious of no wrong, they bring to the field their courage entire; whereas those who believe that the divine power will be angered at their waging an unjust war, by that very conviction—even if no danger should come to meet them from the enemy—are seized beforehand with dread.

Let him try to compress the march of the army into as small a compass as possible, and, if it can be done, let him lead his ranks through such ground that they may not be squeezed together into a narrow column nor, lacking breadth, be drawn out to a great length on the flank.

The same care is to be taken if he himself fears an invasion of the enemy; for surely it is not useful to act and yet unnecessary to guard against suffering, nor urgent to forestall them when they invade hostile territory while leaving unconsidered how to shut out the enemy advancing against himself.
Chapter 8

Wherever he intends to set up his camp for a long time, the enemy not coming out against him—either making his stay for the purpose of ravaging the country, or watching for better opportunities—let him choose ground that is not marshy nor damp; for such places, by their exhalations and the foul smells from the ground, bring sicknesses and plagues upon armies, and have impaired the good health of many and destroyed many, so as to leave an army not merely small but also weak.
Chapter 9

In the winter quarters let him exercise the troops and make them warlike and at home with hardships, allowing them neither to be idle nor to grow slack; for idleness has rendered bodies soft and weak, and slackness has made souls unmanly and cowardly; for pleasures, alluring by their daily familiarity, corrupt the desires even of the most stout-hearted.

Let him first draw them up, distributing the arms to all, that it may be a matter of practice for them to keep their ranks, and that they may become familiar with one another by face and by name—who is under whom, and where, and after how many—and let him teach the extensions and contractions and the wheelings to left and to right, and the shifting of companies, and intervals and closings-up, and the passing-out and passing-in of one through another, and the dividing into companies, and the bringing-down, and the deployment into line and the contraction into depth, and the double-fronted battle, when those in the rear wheel about and fight against the encircling enemy, and let him teach the recalls.

For it has come about that throughout the whole inhabited world there are many and various kinds of places, and it is unclear in what sort each will do battle; and men have experience of their own country,

And in general the forethought of such matters is not to be reckoned a small thing nor to be overlooked; for soldiers who have eaten moderately, so as not to load the belly with much fullness, are more vigorous for battle; for often armies have been defeated for this very reason, their strength failing through want, when the issue of the battle is not decided at a critical moment but reaches its conclusion through the whole day.
Chapter 13

For the looks of the commanders reshape the souls of those under them; and when the general is in good spirits and looks cheerful, the camp too takes heart, as though there were nothing terrible; but when he is cowed and grieved, they sink together in their minds, as though some great evil were appearing before them.

Both befall armies—both to be so dismayed by the enemy as to dare nothing, and so to despise them as to guard against nothing; and the general must be fitted to either, and know when to make the enemy seem mean, both in word and in appearance, and when to make them seem terrible and more fearsome.
The attacks of the light-armed by the wing do more harm to the enemy, casting from the flanks and forcing their way to strike at the exposed parts.

If the support of light-armed be on both sides, let them first, before the hand-to-hand battle, skirmish against the opponents, or, after the phalanx has closed, running up from the flanks, let them make full use of their missiles; for they are driven together into a narrow space and are no less thrown into confusion by such weapons of defence.
Chapter 21

Let him, however, make the rear strong, and those at the side of the wings no weaker than the front-rank men; for those in the rear hinder encirclements no less than those extended on the wing, if either the general, forestalling the danger, spread out the rear and, bringing them up along the wings of the phalanx, station those behind on both sides facing the enemy, or order those already encircled, leaning their backs against the backs of those in front, to make the battle face both ways.

There might be something even more useful than this: to send out, farther from the line by however many stadia he thinks sufficient, some part of his own army, unseen by the enemy, ordering them, when he engages the foe, then, learning it from the scouts, to rise up and hasten on; and this is especially to be done when an expected reinforcement is delayed past its time; for the enemy, supposing these to be that reinforcement and that allies have come from somewhere to their opponents, would perhaps, even while they are still approaching, before the attackers close, rush into flight, thinking that not so great a multitude as it is, but a greater, is coming on.

And these things he must shout out in such a way that the enemy too may overhear; for the friendly hear of their own as more glorious and take fresh courage and become doubled in their zeal, while the foe, learning of their own losses, sink together in their minds, so that sometimes they even rush into flight the moment they receive such a report.

He must tell the foremost officers, and they report it to those next them, then these to those behind, and so on in order down to the last, the first signifying it to those at their heels; for thus quickly and in good order and in quiet they will know it, the order coming to pass much like the beacon-fires.

This is most useful, too, against allied nations of foreign tongue; for, being able neither to speak nor to understand a foreign language, they distinguish friend and foe by the countersign itself. Let these be given even when they are not about to fight, in the camps, against unforeseen disturbances.
Chapter 27

Let them, at the onsets, in a mass, before coming to close quarters, hold their swords aloft above their heads, repeatedly slanting them toward the sun; for burnished spear-points and bright swords flashing one upon another in answer to the sunlight send forth before the battle a terrible lightning; and if these things are done also among the enemy, one must dismay them in return, but if not, dismay them beforehand.

Let some soldiers be left also at the palisade, both to guard the camp and to watch over the baggage, lest the enemy's general, perceiving it to be empty, send men to plunder what is in it and seize the position.
Chapter 32
For where one must either conquer and prevail, or, being defeated, perish utterly, how could anyone bear witness either to prudence in the victory or to deliberate choice in the defeat?

And just as, if a helmsman, leaving the tiller, should himself do what the sailors must do, the vessel would come into danger, so, if a general, leaving off counselling by judgement, should come down to the tasks of the soldiers, the unsteered neglect of the whole would render useless the more necessary help.

Let the honours be both those according to ancestral usage and according to the customs prevailing among each people; but these are a general's honours: suits of armour, ornaments, gifts from the spoils, commands of fifty, of a hundred, captaincies, leaderships of companies, and the other commands lawful among each people; for the lesser authorities to private men who have shown valour, the greater commands to officers who have proved the best; for these are both magnanimous rewards to those who have already done a noble deed and necessary incitements to those who desire the same.
But if there be need of money and of great common expense, let him proclaim that everything driven and carried off be brought up to himself.

For each of the soldiers, seeing with his own eyes that he himself would be neglected, had he chanced to fall, and divining the future—that not even he himself, if he should die, would be buried—takes ill the outrage of being left untombed.
For one must neither be faithless to compacts, nor be himself the first to do anything impious, but suspicious, so as to guard against the enemy's hidden treachery;

But whoever, on becoming master of a city, deals harshly and warlike at once, plundering or killing or razing it, makes the other cities more estranged, so as to render the war for himself toilsome and the victory hard to hope for;

For sometimes one of the traitors has agreed to open the gates, or to cut down some of those in the city who oppose, or to attack the garrison of the enemy within, at the third or fourth or whatever hour of the night one may think opportune; and then one of two things has happened: either the enemy's army, drawing near sooner than it should, has been detected before the traitors are ready, and so has been hindered from the undertaking, or, coming too late, has become the cause of death to the traitors, who are detected, while himself accomplishing nothing of what was proposed.

watches the plotter more closely; for he who thinks himself outside danger does some one of his designs whenever it seems good to him, while he who is in the very danger seeks to act first, whenever he gets the chance; therefore the besieger must secure his own camp by ditch and palisade and guards.

Assaults by night are for the most part useful to besiegers; for to those within, unable to see what is happening because of the darkness, the proceedings seem more terrible, and they are compelled to form a harsher anticipation than the things actually being done, whence arise confusions and tumults, no one being able to keep his head in such circumstances, but many even saying that things not being done are happening, and being able to know neither where they will attack, nor how many, nor with what parts; but there are runnings to and fro hither and thither, and shouts, and amazements full of panic confusion.
Chapter 42

If the general be eager to accomplish something by main force, let him not shrink from being himself the first seen in the doing; for men do not so much do anything when compelled by the threats of their superiors as when shamed by the example of the more venerable; for seeing the leader the first to set his hand to it, a man both learns that he must make haste and is ashamed not to do it and afraid to disobey; and the multitude is no longer disposed as toward one commanded like a slave, but is moved as toward one summoned on equal terms.

Therefore, even if what I have composed should appear to many to be matter already familiar, I would on that very account take pleasure, since I have not merely set down precepts of generalship but have also aimed at the art of generalship and the practical wisdom that lies within these matters; and I should count myself fortunate if I were judged by such men to be capable of comprehending in words those things which the Romans have accomplished by their power and through their deeds.
Temperate, since he is about to attain so great a command; for undisciplined impulses, once they acquire the power to do as they please, become uncontrollable in their desires.

Let him appoint captains and tribunes and commanders of a thousand, and any other officers he may think he needs, choosing those most loyal to their country, most trustworthy, most vigorous; and after these qualities nothing prevents his choosing also the richest and the best-born.

Yet let him be neither so unstable in mind as to distrust himself altogether, nor so self-willed as not to think that something better than his own thought may be conceived by another; for such a man must either, attending to everyone and nothing to himself, do much that is disadvantageous, or, listening little to others and trusting wholly to himself, fall into many grave errors.
Chapter 4

For this reason the general should, by speech and by embassies, first make demands both of what he wishes to obtain and of what he will not yield, so that, by their refusal to concede what is demanded, the enemy may appear to compel him, and that he may seem to lead out his force to war not by his own choice; and he should call the divine power to witness that he advances without offence, neither despising what those who go to war are wont to suffer, nor having resolved by every means to do the enemy harm.

For such columns become more vulnerable to the sudden appearances of the enemy and least effective. For if the enemy meet them in front, drawn up in greater breadth, they easily rout them, as men in battle surround those who are on a wing; and if they attack the centre of the force from the flank, they quickly tear apart and cut through the column—for when these wheel into a phalanx to defend themselves, the fight becomes weak and lacks depth—and if they attack the rear, the fighting in the rear is terrible and carries evident destruction; and even if they dare to wheel into a front, the same battle befalls them as those drawn up in the van; for the enemy quickly surround them.

Therefore let him not lead the men far from their toils; for when after an interval they are compelled to go to warlike work, they neither go out gladly nor hold out long, but, grown soft in their way of life, they quickly take fright before they have even tried the dangers, and quickly, even after trying them, withdraw, being able neither to hope for nor to endure the perils.
Chapter 10

For just as, in the case of musical instruments, those who are beginning to learn place their fingers upon the holes of the pipes and the intervals of the strings, and often set one finger on one note and another on another, not according to the harmonic interval, then, having with difficulty stretched them out, slowly raise their fingers and slowly set them down; whereas those practised in music, with a hand now effortlessly attuned to rhythm, transfer them swiftly wherever they wish—to check the breath, or to open it, or to pluck a string—so it is that those unaccustomed and untrained in formation, amid much confusion and scarcely avoiding collision with one another, fall into their places, consuming much time, whereas those well drilled move to their formation swiftly, as if of themselves, filling out a harmonious and beautiful sight.

but do not know a foreign land. Often, if a general, hearing that the enemy are a day's march away, breaks camp and leads his army, hastening to come to battle with the enemy, while they withdraw on purpose and do not stand, as though in dread, he follows; and when they keep doing the same thing, until they come to difficult ground and places enclosed by mountains, he presses on, suspecting nothing, then, having plunged into such places, he is shut off by the enemy from the entrance by which the army came in; and they, having seized both the passages forward and held all the heights round about, as in some hunting-net have bound the enemy fast; while he, advancing, was carried on by his impetus, thinking that he was pressing upon a foe avoiding battle, whom on approaching he did not recognize; but afterwards, looking round about him—before and behind and on the flank—and seeing all full of enemies, he was either shot down together with his army, or, unable to fight his way out and refusing to surrender, destroyed all by famine, or, surrendering, made the enemy masters to dispose of them as they would.

Therefore one should manage the cheerfulness of the multitude more by the expression of his face than console it by words; for many have distrusted words as feigned to suit the moment, but, thinking a confident look to be without pretence, they have given credit to the fearlessness. Best of all is the knowledge that comes from both—of saying what one must, and of being seen as one must.
Chapter 14

When a battle is imminent, when the armies, holding the decision of the war uncertain, are thrown into confusion by fear, if the general be able somehow to take prisoners—either from an ambush, or after skirmishing, or men who have strayed from their own camp—then, if he find some noble in spirit and in body, let him either kill them at once on taking them, or, binding them, hand them over to those appointed to keep guard over such, that not many may see the men; but if they be weak and ignoble and mean-spirited, let him further threaten them in his own tent and, having enslaved their souls by fear, lead them out before the multitude weeping and entreating, at the same time saying and pointing out to the soldiers how ignoble and abject and worthless they are, and that it is against such men that they have their battle, men so dreading death, clinging to their knees and grovelling at each man's feet.

The defence against the sling is the most difficult of those among the light-armed; for the lead, being of the same colour as the air, escapes notice as it flies, so as to fall unforeseen upon the unguarded bodies of the enemy; and the impact itself being violent, and the missile, heated by friction with the air as it whizzes, sinks as deep as possible into the flesh, so as not even to be seen, and the swelling quickly closes over it.
Chapter 20

A shrewd general, seeing the enemy many while he himself is about to risk a battle with fewer soldiers, has chosen and contrived to obtain such positions as these, in which either, drawing up along a river-bank, he repels the enemy's encirclement on that side, or, choosing a mountain-skirt, he shuts off by the very mountains those who wish to outflank him, stationing a few on the heights to prevent the enemy from getting above his head.

And besides, even in the dangers themselves, the appearances of enemies not before encountered strike the soul with panic; for, anticipating something worse than they will suffer, men await the future as more fearsome.

If at any time he wishes to break camp by night without the enemy's knowledge—either purposing to seize positions beforehand, or fleeing those he holds, or as yet unwilling to come to the necessity of fighting—let him withdraw after burning many fires; for the enemy, seeing the lights, suppose that he remains in his place, but if the camp meanwhile becomes unlighted, they take up a suspicion that they are fleeing, and send out ambushes beforehand and pursue.

Therefore there is every necessity that they, worn out and getting not a single hour's rest, but distressed with sleeplessness and toils, and then exhausted with a view to what is to come, defend their own more weakly, or send out men to beg and to surrender the city.

Let him take thought for the market and for the convoy of merchants both by land and by sea, that, their coming being free from danger, they may without hesitation bring up their freight of provisions.

He must be of good repute, because the multitude chafes at being subject to the disreputable; for no one willingly submits to taking as his master and commander a man worse than himself.

The palisades on the mountains and hills, unless they are everywhere continuous, appear larger than those on level ground, but contain fewer men than the sight would suggest; for many parts within are left empty of men; for in such places there must of necessity be many pits, and many precipitous and rough and untentable places, while the palisade, being set before the men, reasonably extends in length.

By money-getter I mean the usurer, the petty trader, the merchant, or those who do anything like these things; for such men must of necessity be small-minded, fluttered about gain and consumed with anxiety over the acquisition of money, and so have had no part at all in noble pursuits.

When the sacrifices are favourable, let him begin every undertaking, and let him call all the officers to the sight of the victims, that, having seen them, they may bid those under them be of good courage, reporting that the gods command them to fight; for the forces take great heart when they think they go out against the dangers with the gods' consent; for they themselves, each privately, watch closely and observe both signs and voices, and the favourable sacrifice on behalf of all has revived even those who privately were despondent.
A good man, therefore, is not only the best leader of his country and of the body of soldiers, but also no senseless general with regard to his own lasting good repute, kept ever free from danger.

If, on the contrary, the sacrifices turn out unfavourable, let him remain where he is, and, even if something presses hard, let him endure every inconvenience—for he can suffer nothing worse than what the divine power foretells—since, if anything better than the present is to come, the sacrifices must of necessity become favourable; but let him sacrifice often on the same day; for a single hour and a moment of time has either harmed those who acted too soon or those who acted too late.
